newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela jail fire may go unpunished - rights group.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela jail fire may go unpunished - rights group.

text.p: As the painstaking process of identifying 25 burned bodies from Venezuela's jail fire continues, human rights groups voiced concern on Thursday that the guards who apparently started the fire may go unpunished.

Prison officials and inmates have said Tuesday's fire was started by guards who locked a group of inmates into a small cell and threw in tear gas and incendiary devices. But rights activists said even overwhelming evidence may not be enough to bring those responsible to justice.
"Our fear is that after one to two years they will be free," Raul Cubas, general coordinator of local rights group Provea, told Reuters.

The guards on duty at the time of the incident were arrested on Wednesday. Prisoners at La Planta jail in the southwestern outskirts of Caracas said the fire began after an argument between inmates and guards during an early morning roll call. About 40 inmates were trapped in the small cell.
"They tell us that the guards threw tear gas canisters into a highly crowded area where there were a lot of inflammable materials," said Liliana Ortega, executive director of rights group Cofavic.
Some prisoners managed to crawl to safety through a small hole in the roof. The rest died engulfed in flames.

The mother of one of the 25 victims said guards had told inmates last week that they would carry out a massacre. "He told us that they were afraid because a guard told them he was going to burn them alive," Carmen Sanchez told Union Radio.
Morgue officials said they had identified only nine of the 25 charred and twisted bodies recovered from the cell. Burns were so severe that relatives have not been able to recognise their loved ones.
"I went to identify my brother but it's impossible. What I saw was a piece of coal, it (the body) doesn't even have hands," Carmen Luisa Alvarado said on Wednesday.

Experts blamed the tragedy on critical overcrowding at the jail. Built over 30 years ago to house 550 inmates, La Planta currently holds about 1,700, prison officials said. About 70 percent of inmates have not been sentenced, they added.

"It's the most overcrowded jail in Venezuela and an overcrowded jail is a time bomb," criminologist Elio Gomez said. The presence of national guardsmen within such an environment creates an explosive cocktail, he added.
"The armed forces should not be working in the prisons. Jails are not prisoner camps."
The National Guard has provided additional security at Venezuela's violence-prone prisons for several years.
Apart from the military trial, two civil courts have opened investigations into the tragedy, creating confusion and a conflict of interests, activists said.

No officials have been punished for previous tragedies in Venezuela's jails despite compelling evidence that guards were involved, Cubas noted. "As normally justice here doesn't punish officials who violate human rights, they don't fear the consequences of their actions," he said.
Venezuela's overcrowded and decaying prisons, considered to be among the most dangerous in Latin America, are frequent scenes of violence between inmates and clashes with guards.

The tragedy at La Planta was the worst in Venezuela's jails since about 120 prisoners were burned or hacked to death with machetes during a gang fight at the Sabaneta jail in the western city of Maracaibo in January 1994.
